transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2025-05-20
- Time: 15:00 UTC (48 minutes)
- Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neal (Redwood Product), Maya Thompson (Summit Head of AI), Ethan Zhao (Summit Sr ML Eng), Jordan Blake (Product), Rosa Lin (Security)

Summary: Quick walkthrough of Redwood Console and Optimize focused on prompt-set driven quality monitoring, how regression alerts are configured, and traffic split mechanic for A/B comparisons. Discussed tradeoffs (latency vs cost, hosted vs dedicated), security questions around KMS and audit logs, and pilot next steps.

---
00:00 Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we, uh, really appreciate you taking the time. Quick roll call?
00:08 Maya Thompson: Hi, Maya here, thanks Alex.
00:10 Ethan Zhao: Ethan on the call.
00:11 Jordan Blake: Jordan here.
00:12 Rosa Lin: Rosa, security.
00:14 Priya Desai: Priya from Redwood, I'll be doing most of the demo.
00:16 Liam O'Neal: Liam from Product, hi.
00:18 Alex Kim: Great, objective for today — walk through how we instrument prompt sets, set regression alerts, and run traffic splits for A/B comparisons. We'll show Console and a quick bit of Optimize recommendations.

01:05 Priya Desai: Alright jumping into the Console, so this is a sample Summit Retail org — we created a prompt set called "checkout-returnability-v2" to capture common customer support prompts, we attach golden labels and scoring thresholds here. Uh, quick note, the transcription might say "golden" but in the product it's labelled as reference responses.

02:30 Ethan Zhao: Quick interrupt — in our stack we currently hit a variety of models. Latency needs to be under 400ms for the storefront bot, throughput spikes at 200 TPS. How does the quality tooling play with throughput?

02:50 Priya Desai: Good question. The Console is mostly orthogonal — evaluations run off sampled traffic, you can do continuous sampling at 1% or 10% depending on cost. Optimize will recommend batching and quant profiles that reduce per-token cost and change latency by a predictable amount. For the traffic spike, you can pair Dedicated capacity with autoscaling. If you go hosted, we'd suggest prefix caching and a lower sampling for evals to keep costs sane.

04:12 Jordan Blake: When you say sampling, is that before or after KV cache and batching? We saw variability depending on where sampling hooks into the request.

04:28 Priya Desai: The sampling occurs at the routing layer before batching aggregation so you get true production latencies in the traces but it's configurable — we can sample post-cache for a subset if you want to measure cold vs warm cache behavior.

05:35 Maya Thompson: Let's talk signals — what types of regressions do you detect? We care about answer correctness, hallucination, and tone.

05:44 Priya Desai: We support behavioral metrics (BLEU-ish, token overlap), classifier-based checks, and custom heuristics you can write against the SDK. The default regression alert can be set on a rolling window — e.g., a 3-sigma drop in average correctness over 24 hours. You can also tie alerts to specific prompt sets.

06:58 Rosa Lin: On security, we need to know where logs live, how long telemetry is retained, and whether prompts are stored unencrypted. We have KMS policies and audit requirements.

07:12 Alex Kim: Short answer: audit logs and token-level traces are optional and configurable. For Private deployments we can integrate with your KMS/HSM and retain logs on your VPC. Hosted customers get encrypted-at-rest logs with customer-specific keys. We'll follow up with SOC2 artefacts.

08:25 Ethan Zhao: Any SLA differences between Dedicated and Hosted for latency we should expect?

08:33 Liam O'Neal: Dedicated gives you predictable throughput with an SLA on p50/p95 latency ranges; hosted is best-effort with soft guarantees but usually lower time-to-market. We'll put the expected latency bands in the sizing worksheet.

09:10 Priya Desai: Back to the demo — here's how to author a prompt set. You can upload a CSV of prompts, map expected outputs, add evaluation rules, and tag templates for segmentation.

11:00 Priya Desai: Ok watch this: I create a regression alert bound to the prompt set "checkout-returnability-v2" with a threshold for the semantic-score dropping below 0.78 for three consecutive windows. You can set notification hooks to PagerDuty, Slack, or webhook.

12:05 Jordan Blake: Can we tune sensitivity? We want to avoid too many noisy alerts.

12:15 Priya Desai: Yep, you get a sensitivity slider and a dry-run mode where alerts will log but not notify. Also the system suggests thresholds based on historical variance — Optimize computes an expected delta and recommends initial thresholds.

13:20 Maya Thompson: Show us A/B traffic splits — we want to compare the new quantized variant with the current production model.

13:30 Priya Desai: Sure. In Console you pick a route, create an experiment, pick the control and candidate models — in this case control is redwood-gptx-prod, candidate is redwood-gptx-q4f — set split percentages and rollout windows. You can tie the split to a prompt set so only those prompts are evaluated.

14:45 Ethan Zhao: If the candidate triggers a regression alert do you automatically rollback traffic?

14:52 Priya Desai: You can set automatic rollback policies: immediate rollback on severe regression, or gradual rollback with a canary. We also support model fallback to a higher fidelity variant if latency SLOs are missed.

16:10 Jordan Blake: For A/B, what metrics are surfaced? We'll need token-level cost, p95 latency, and semantic score distribution.

16:22 Priya Desai: Exactly — the experiment dashboard shows relative lift/loss for each metric with confidence intervals, and per-prompt breakdown so you can find specific prompt buckets that caused differences. There's also a pairwise comparison view for reviewer ops.

18:05 Maya Thompson: Can we export the raw evaluation data to our data warehouse for offline analysis?

18:13 Liam O'Neal: Yes, export hooks to S3/BigQuery, and an API to pull raw eval traces. We recommend periodic batch exports for long-term retention.

19:30 Rosa Lin: Audit-wise, we need immutable logs for model changes and eval configs. Is that supported?

19:40 Alex Kim: Yes — Console maintains an audit trail for runbooks, experiments, and threshold changes. In Private deployments those logs can be stored on-prem or forwarded to your SIEM.

21:05 Ethan Zhao: A couple implementation questions: how much infra effort is a Private deployment? Our infra team is small.

21:16 Priya Desai: Private has an installer and operator pattern; typical on-prem pilot is 4–6 weeks including networking and KMS integration. For VPC-hosted Private we can do it faster since we don't touch your on-prem hardware. We'll scope based on your compliance needs.

22:30 Jordan Blake: Can Optimize automatically recommend quantization profiles per workload? We tried a blanket q4 earlier and saw big quality delta on hard prompts.

22:44 Priya Desai: Optimize runs synthetic bench and lightweight calibration on a sample of your prompt set. It will suggest per-model quant profiles and give an expected delta in semantic score. You can run a constrained sweep if you want to target p95 latency under X ms.

24:10 Maya Thompson: Let's do a short scenario — we deploy candidate model q4f on 10% traffic for 48 hours. What should we watch for operationally?

24:25 Priya Desai: Good scenario. Steps: 1) tie the experiment to the prompt set, 2) set regression thresholds, 3) enable dry-run alerts for first 6 hours, 4) route 10% production traffic, 5) stream eval traces to your BI, 6) decide on auto-rollback or manual. Watch for tail latency, semantic score drift, and increased failed responses.

26:12 Ethan Zhao: If we see a small drop in semantic score but 30% cost reduction, would that be surfaced as a tradeoff?

26:20 Priya Desai: Yes, the experiment view highlights cost savings vs quality delta and you can set a weighted scoring function if your product cares more about cost. We also have a threshold enforcement to prevent automatic rollout if quality drops beyond a business rule.

28:00 Jordan Blake: How intrusive is the SDK to our app? We already have an in-house wrapper.

28:08 Priya Desai: The SDK is lightweight — HTTP/SDK calls and a sidecar option for easier migration. For traffic-splitting we provide a routing client or a header-based split you can attach at your edge.

29:30 Maya Thompson: Any gotchas with multi-region deployments? We need EU data residency for some markets.

29:40 Liam O'Neal: You can pin experiments and eval storage to regions. For hosted customers we provide region specific endpoints; for Private, obviously you control residency.

31:10 Rosa Lin: We need to validate that exported traces do not contain PII; can we run built-in redaction?

31:20 Priya Desai: Yes, there's a redaction pipeline with regex and model-based PII scrubbers. You can choose to redact at capture or at rest, and redact before exporting.

32:55 Ethan Zhao: Let's talk pilot scope — what would you recommend given our constraints (400ms p95, 200 TPS spikes, small infra team)?

33:05 Alex Kim: For Summit Retail we'd suggest a 6-week pilot: week 0–1 onboarding and security review, week 2–3 traffic-split experiments with 1% and 10% sampling, week 4–5 scale tests on Dedicated or VPC, week 6 review and decision. We'll size Dedicated capacity for 200 TPS peak with headroom.

34:30 Jordan Blake: Pricing?

34:35 Alex Kim: I'll send pilot pricing — short version: usage fees for hosted; fixed monthly for Dedicated pilot + small onboarding professional services. We'll include the Optimize credits for the pilot.

35:50 Maya Thompson: Regarding regressions, how often are alerts false positives? We, uh, had noisy alerts in previous tools.

36:02 Priya Desai: The combination of suggested thresholds, dry-run mode, and the classifier-based filters reduces noise. We also support human-in-the-loop confirmations so the first N alerts won't trigger auto rollback until reviewed.

37:20 Ethan Zhao: Is there a baked-in reviewer UI for pairwise comparisons?

37:28 Priya Desai: Yes, the pairwise reviewer shows two responses side-by-side with diffs and an easy accept/reject flow that feeds back into your metric labels.

38:45 Maya Thompson: Ok good. A couple security specifics: we need SAML SSO, RBAC with least privilege, and pageable audit exports.

38:55 Alex Kim: Supported — SAML, SCIM, RBAC, and exports — we'll share the security pack; Rosa you'll get the SOC2 and architecture docs.

40:12 Jordan Blake: On a practical note, can we seed our prompt sets with annotations from customer support transcripts?

40:20 Priya Desai: Absolutely, you can upload CSVs, or call the API to bulk create items. We recommend sampling from production logs then human-labeling a 2k example set to start.

41:40 Ethan Zhao: If we need an on-prem Private pilot, what's the approximate baseline infra — GPUs, nodes?

41:52 Liam O'Neal: For a pilot supporting 200 TPS at 400ms with batching you'd likely need 4 high-end GPUs with room for autoscaling; we'll provide a Dedicated sizing worksheet with concrete numbers.

43:05 Maya Thompson: Let's confirm the next steps and owners.

43:12 Alex Kim: I'll send the Dedicated sizing worksheet and pilot pricing. Priya will share the Console how-to video and a short runbook. Ethan you'll upload the sample prompt set and traces. Rosa will give us the security contact.

44:30 Jordan Blake: Anything else?

44:35 Ethan Zhao: One last thing — can the regression alerts post to our internal incident channel and include trace link?

44:42 Priya Desai: Yes, webhook/Slack/PagerDuty integrations support a trace link and masked payload.

45:10 Maya Thompson: Sounds good, thanks everyone.

45:15 Alex Kim: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the artifacts.

45:25 Meeting end.
